title: Schloss Gripsholm
author: Kurt Tucholsky
source: http://www.zeno.org/Literatur/M/Tucholsky,+Kurt/Werke/1931/Schlo%C3%9F+Gripsholm (Zeno.org, chapters 1–5; text of Kurt Tucholsky: Gesammelte Werke in zehn Bänden, Bd. 9, Reinbek 1975; licence: gemeinfrei)
orthography: modernised to current German spelling (dass, muss, bisschen, Fantasie, Gestern Abend, ...); wording unchanged; page numbers and section numbers removed; three scan typos fixed (l2% → 12%, and two commas that should be full stops). Lydia's dialect (Missingsch/Low German) is kept exactly as Tucholsky wrote it.
intro_en: Kurt Tucholsky (1890–1935) was one of the sharpest and funniest journalists in 1920s Berlin. 'Schloss Gripsholm' (1931) is his light summer story: the narrator Peter and his girlfriend Lydia go on holiday to Sweden, near Gripsholm Castle. It opens with a comic exchange of letters with his real publisher, Ernst Rowohlt, and then becomes a witty, warm love story full of natural spoken German. Heads-up: Lydia sometimes speaks Missingsch, a northern German dialect mix – enjoy it, but don't copy those spellings.

8 June
Dear Mr Tucholsky,
Many thanks for your letter of 2 June. We have made a note of your request. Something different for today.
As you know, I have recently published all sorts of political books, which you have certainly dealt with at length. But now I'd really like to look after 'fine literature' again for once.
units.explain_en: The novel begins with letters between Tucholsky and his real publisher, Ernst Rowohlt. German letters start with 'Lieber Herr ...,' and the next line begins with a small letter because it follows a comma. 'andres' is a shortened, old-fashioned form of 'anderes'. 'hinlänglich' is old-fashioned for 'genug' or 'ausreichend'. 'wieder einmal' means 'once again'.

Haben Sie gar nichts? Wie wäre es denn mit einer kleinen Liebesgeschichte? Überlegen Sie sich das mal! Das Buch soll nicht teuer werden, und ich drucke Ihnen für den Anfang zehntausend Stück. Die befreundeten Sortimenter sagen mir jedes Mal auf meinen Reisen, wie gern die Leute so etwas lesen. Wie ist es damit?
Sie haben bei uns noch 46 RM gut – wohin sollen wir Ihnen die überweisen?
Mit den besten Grüßen
Ihr
(Riesenschnörkel) Ernst Rowohlt
units.en:
Haven't you got anything at all? How about a little love story? Think it over! The book shouldn't be expensive, and to start with I'll print ten thousand copies for you. Every time I'm travelling, the booksellers I'm friends with tell me how much people like reading that sort of thing. What do you say?
We still owe you 46 Reichsmarks – where should we transfer the money?
With best wishes
Yours
(huge flourish) Ernst Rowohlt
units.explain_en: 'Wie wäre es mit ...?' is an everyday way to suggest something: 'Wie wär's mit Pizza?' The little word 'mal' in 'Überlegen Sie sich das mal!' makes a command sound friendlier – very common in speech. 'Sortimenter' is an old trade word; today you say 'Buchhändler'. 'Sie haben bei uns noch 46 RM gut' means 'you still have 46 RM credit with us' (RM = Reichsmark, the currency back then). '(Riesenschnörkel)' is Tucholsky joking about Rowohlt's giant signature.

words.note: für den Anfang = to start with
Mit besten Grüßen = best wishes (end of a letter)

10. Juni
Lieber Herr Rowohlt,
Dank für Ihren Brief vom 8. 6.
Ja, eine Liebesgeschichte . . . lieber Meister, wie denken Sie sich das? In der heutigen Zeit Liebe? Lieben Sie? Wer liebt denn heute noch?
Dann schon lieber eine kleine Sommergeschichte.
Die Sache ist nicht leicht. Sie wissen, wie sehr es mir widerstrebt, die Öffentlichkeit mit meinem persönlichen Kram zu behelligen – das fällt also fort.
units.en:
10 June
Dear Mr Rowohlt,
Thanks for your letter of 8/6.
Yes, a love story... my dear master, what are you thinking? Love, in times like these? Are you in love? Who still loves anyone these days?
A little summer story, then, if anything.
It isn't easy. You know how much I hate bothering the public with my personal stuff – so that's out.
units.explain_en: Tucholsky answers ironically. Calling Rowohlt 'Meister' (master) is teasing flattery. 'Dann schon lieber ...' means 'I'd rather ..., then'. 'es widerstrebt mir' is formal for 'I really don't like to' – today you'd say 'Ich mag es gar nicht, ...'. 'behelligen' is old-fashioned for 'belästigen' or 'nerven' (to bother). 'Kram' (stuff) is informal and still very common. 'das fällt fort' – today we say 'das fällt weg' (that's out).

words.en: to be dropped, to be out

units.de:
Außerdem betrüge ich jede Frau mit meiner Schreibmaschine und erlebe daher nichts Romantisches. Und soll ich mir die Geschichte vielleicht ausdenken? Fantasie haben doch nur die Geschäftsleute, wenn sie nicht zahlen können. Dann fällt ihnen viel ein. Unsereinem . . .
Schreibe ich den Leuten nicht ihren Wunschtraum (›Die Gräfin raffte ihre Silber-Robe, würdigte den Grafen keines Blickes und fiel die Schlosstreppe hinunter‹), dann bleibt nur noch das Propplem über die Ehe als Zimmer-Gymnastik, die ›Menschliche Einstellung‹ und all das Zeug, das wir nicht mögen. Woher nehmen und nicht bei Villon stehlen?
units.en:
Besides, I cheat on every woman with my typewriter, so I never experience anything romantic. And am I supposed to make the story up? Only businessmen have imagination – when they can't pay. Then they come up with all sorts of things. People like me...
If I don't write people their dream fantasy ('The countess gathered up her silver gown, didn't deign to look at the count, and fell down the castle stairs'), then all that's left is the Probblem of marriage as indoor gymnastics, 'The Human Approach' and all that stuff we don't like. Where am I supposed to get it from without stealing from Villon?
units.explain_en: 'betrügen' means to cheat (on someone) and is still normal. 'sich etwas ausdenken' (to make something up) and 'einfallen' (to occur to someone: 'Mir fällt nichts ein' = I can't think of anything) are very useful verbs. 'Propplem' is a deliberate misspelling that mocks a pompous way of saying 'Problem'. The countess joke parodies cheap romance novels: she should walk down the stairs, but she 'falls' down them. 'Woher nehmen und nicht stehlen?' is a real idiom (where on earth should I get it?); Tucholsky adds Villon, a French poet other writers liked to borrow from.

units.de:
Da wir grade von Lyrik sprechen:
Wie kommt es, dass Sie in § 9 unsres Verlagsvertrages 15 Prozent honorarfreie Exemplare berechnen? So viel Rezensionsexemplare schicken Sie doch niemals in die Welt hinaus! So jagen Sie den sauern Schweiß Ihrer Autoren durch die Gurgel – kein Wunder, dass Sie auf Samt saufen, während unsereiner auf harten Bänken dünnes Bier schluckt. Aber so ist alles.
Dass Sie mir gut sind, wusste ich. Dass Sie mir für 46 RM gut sind, erfreut mein Herz. Bitte wie gewöhnlich an die alte Adresse. Übrigens fahre ich nächste Woche in Urlaub.
Mit vielen schönen Grüßen
Ihr
Tucholsky
units.en:
Speaking of poetry:
How come that in § 9 of our publishing contract you count 15 per cent royalty-free copies? You never send that many review copies out into the world! That's how you pour your authors' bitter sweat down your throat – no wonder you drink on velvet while people like me swallow thin beer on hard benches. But that's how everything is.
That you're fond of me, I knew. That you're good for 46 RM to me warms my heart. Please send it to the old address as usual. By the way, I'm going on holiday next week.
With very best wishes
Yours
Tucholsky
units.explain_en: 'Da wir grade von ... sprechen' = 'speaking of ...' ('grade' is the spoken form of 'gerade'). 'Wie kommt es, dass ...?' = 'How come ...?' – very useful. He complains about 'honorarfreie Exemplare': copies the author earns nothing on. There's a pun: 'Sie sind mir gut' is old-fashioned for 'you like me', while 'Sie sind mir 46 RM gut' means 'you owe me 46 RM'. 'unsres' is an older short form of 'unseres'. 'saufen' is a rude word for drinking a lot – OK with friends, not with teachers.

words.note: in Urlaub fahren = to go on holiday

Lieber Herr Tucholsky,
vielen Dank für Ihren Brief vom 10. d. M.
Die 15% honorarfreien Exemplare sind – also das können Sie mir wirklich glauben – meine einzige Verdienstmöglichkeit. Lieber Herr Tucholsky, wenn Sie unsre Bilanz sähen, dann wüssten Sie, dass es ein armer Verleger gar nicht leicht hat. Ohne die 15% könnte ich überhaupt nicht existieren und würde glatt verhungern. Das werden Sie doch nicht wollen.
Die Sommergeschichte sollten Sie sich durch den Kopf gehn lassen.
units.en:
Ernst Rowohlt Publishing House
Berlin W 50
Passauer Strasse 8/9
12 June
Dear Mr Tucholsky,
many thanks for your letter of the 10th of this month.
The 15% royalty-free copies are – and you really can believe me on this – my only way of making money. Dear Mr Tucholsky, if you saw our balance sheet, you'd know that a poor publisher really doesn't have an easy time. Without the 15% I couldn't exist at all and would simply starve. Surely you don't want that.
You should give the summer story some thought.
units.explain_en: 'd. M.' stands for 'dieses Monats' (of this month), an old business abbreviation. 'wenn Sie ... sähen, dann wüssten Sie' is Konjunktiv II ('if you saw, you would know'); in everyday speech people say 'wenn Sie ... sehen würden, dann würden Sie wissen'. 'glatt' here means 'simply, flat out'. 'sich etwas durch den Kopf gehen lassen' (to think something over) is a very common idiom; 'gehn' is just the spoken form of 'gehen'. 'doch' in 'Das werden Sie doch nicht wollen' adds 'surely'.

Die Leute wollen neben der Politik und dem Aktuellen etwas haben, was sie ihrer Freundin schenken können. Sie glauben gar nicht, wie das fehlt. Ich denke an eine kleine Geschichte, nicht zu umfangreich, etwa 15 – 16 Bogen, zart im Gefühl, kartoniert, leicht ironisch und mit einem bunten Umschlag. Der Inhalt kann so frei sein, wie Sie wollen. Ich würde Ihnen vielleicht insoweit entgegenkommen, dass ich die honorarfreien Exemplare auf 14% heruntersetze.
Wie gefällt Ihnen unser neuer Verlagskatalog?
Ich wünsche Ihnen einen vergnügten Urlaub und bin mit vielen Grüßen
Ihr
(Riesenschnörkel) Ernst Rowohlt
units.en:
Besides politics and current affairs, people want something they can give their girlfriend. You wouldn't believe how much that's missing. I'm thinking of a little story, not too long, about 15–16 printed sheets, delicate in feeling, with a card cover, lightly ironic and with a colourful jacket. The content can be as free as you like. I might meet you halfway to the extent of lowering the royalty-free copies to 14%.
How do you like our new catalogue?
I wish you a happy holiday and remain, with best wishes,
Yours
(huge flourish) Ernst Rowohlt
units.explain_en: 'neben' here means 'besides' or 'apart from'. 'Sie glauben gar nicht, wie ...' = 'You wouldn't believe how ...' – great for conversations. 'Bogen' is a printing term (one big sheet folded into 16 pages). 'jemandem entgegenkommen' means to meet someone halfway, and it's still common. 'Wie gefällt Ihnen ...?' (How do you like ...?) is one of the most useful questions in German. 'vergnügt' sounds a bit old-fashioned; today: 'einen schönen Urlaub'.

words.note: Wie gefällt dir ...? = How do you like ...?

15. Juni
Lieber Meister Rowohlt,
auf dem neuen Verlagskatalog hat Sie Gulbransson ganz richtig gezeichnet: still sinnend an des Baches Rand sitzen Sie da und angeln die fetten Fische. Der Köder mit 14% honorarfreier Exemplare ist nicht fett genug – 12 sind auch ganz schön. Denken Sie mal ein bisschen darüber nach und geben Sie Ihrem harten Verlegerherzen einen Stoß. Bei 14% fällt mir bestimmt nichts ein – ich dichte erst ab 12%.
units.en:
15 June
Dear Master Rowohlt,
on the new catalogue Gulbransson has drawn you exactly right: you sit there, quietly musing by the edge of the brook, angling for the fat fish. The bait of 14% royalty-free copies isn't fat enough – 12 is pretty nice too. Think it over a little and give your hard publisher's heart a nudge. At 14% I definitely won't come up with anything – I only write poetry from 12% up.
units.explain_en: Olaf Gulbransson was a famous cartoonist. 'still sinnend an des Baches Rand' quotes the poem by Theodor Storm at the very start of the book. 'an des Baches Rand' is poetic word order – normal German is 'am Rand des Baches'. 'angeln' = to fish with a rod, 'der Köder' = bait. 'einen Stoß geben' = to give a push. 'dichten' means to write poetry – he jokes that he only gets creative at a better percentage.

Ich schreibe diesen Brief schon mit einem Fuß in der Bahn. In einer Stunde fahre ich ab – nach Schweden. Ich will in diesem Urlaub überhaupt nicht arbeiten, sondern ich möchte in die Bäume gucken und mich mal richtig ausruhn.
Wenn ich zurückkomme, wollen wir den Fall noch einmal bebrüten. Nun aber schwenke ich meinen Hut, grüße Sie recht herzlich und wünsche Ihnen einen guten Sommer! Und vergessen Sie nicht: 12%!
Mit vielen schönen Grüßen
Ihr getreuer
Tucholsky
units.en:
I'm writing this letter with one foot on the train already. In an hour I leave – for Sweden. I don't want to do any work at all on this holiday; I want to look at the trees and have a really good rest.
When I get back, let's mull the matter over again. But now I wave my hat, send you my warmest regards and wish you a good summer! And don't forget: 12%!
With very best wishes
Yours faithfully
Tucholsky
units.explain_en: 'die Bahn' is the railway or train (today you'd say 'mit einem Fuß im Zug'). 'nicht ..., sondern ...' = 'not ..., but rather ...' – an important structure. 'gucken' is everyday German for 'schauen' (to look). 'ausruhn' is the spoken form of 'ausruhen'. 'bebrüten' literally means 'to sit on eggs' like a hen – a joke; today you'd say 'besprechen' (discuss). 'Ihr getreuer' (yours faithfully) is old-fashioned.

Unterschrieben – zugeklebt – frankiert – es war genau acht Uhr zehn Minuten. Um neun Uhr zwanzig ging der Zug von Berlin nach Kopenhagen. Und nun wollten wir ja wohl die Prinzessin abholen.
Sie hatte eine Altstimme und hieß Lydia.
Karlchen und Jakopp aber nannten jede Frau, mit der einer von uns dreien zu tun hatte, ›die Prinzessin‹, um den betreffenden Prinzgemahl zu ehren – und dies war nun also die Prinzessin; aber keine andre durfte je mehr so genannt werden.

units.en:
Signed – sealed – stamped – it was exactly ten past eight. At twenty past nine the train left Berlin for Copenhagen. And now, I suppose, it was time to pick up the princess.
She had a contralto voice and her name was Lydia.
Karlchen and Jakopp, however, called every woman that any of us three had anything to do with 'the princess', to honour the prince consort in question – and so this was now the princess; but no other woman was ever to be called that again.
She wasn't a princess.
units.explain_en: Now the story begins. The three past participles 'unterschrieben – zugeklebt – frankiert' give a quick rhythm ('frankieren' = to put stamps on; today 'eine Briefmarke draufkleben'). 'abholen' (to pick someone up) is very common. 'hieß Lydia' comes from 'heißen' (to be called). Karlchen and Jakopp are the narrator's two best friends. 'andre' is short for 'andere'. 'mit jemandem zu tun haben' = to have something to do with someone.

Der Mann führte den Titel eines Generalkonsuls und handelte ansonsten mit Seifen. Immer lagen da Pakete im Büro herum, und so hatte der Dicke wenigstens eine Ausrede, wenn seine Hände fettig waren.
Der Generalkonsul hatte ihr in einer Anwandlung fürstlicher Freigebigkeit fünf Wochen Urlaub gewährt; er fuhr nach Abbazia. Gestern Abend war er abgefahren – werde ihm der Schlafwagen leicht! Im Büro saßen sein Schwager und für Lydia eine Stellvertreterin. Was gingen mich denn seine Seifen an – Lydia ging mich an.
units.en:
The man held the title of Consul General and otherwise dealt in soaps. There were always packages lying around the office, so the fat man at least had an excuse when his hands were greasy.
In a fit of princely generosity the Consul General had given her five weeks' holiday; he was going to Abbazia. He had left last night – may the sleeping car lie lightly upon him! His brother-in-law and a stand-in for Lydia were sitting in the office. What did his soaps matter to me – Lydia mattered to me.
units.explain_en: 'handeln mit' = to trade in or deal in. 'die Ausrede' (excuse) is common. 'werde ihm der Schlafwagen leicht!' parodies the funeral phrase 'Möge ihm die Erde leicht sein' (may the earth lie lightly on him) – a dark joke. Abbazia is a seaside resort, today Opatija in Croatia. 'Was gehen mich ... an?' means 'What has ... got to do with me?' – compare the everyday phrase 'Das geht dich nichts an!' (That's none of your business!).

Da stand sie schon mit den Koffern vor ihrem Haus –
»Hallo!«
»Du bischa all do?« sagte die Prinzessin – zur grenzenlosen Verwunderung des Taxichauffeurs, der dieses für ostchinesisch hielt. Es war aber missingsch.
Missingsch ist das, was herauskommt, wenn ein Plattdeutscher hochdeutsch sprechen will. Er krabbelt auf der glatt gebohnerten Treppe der deutschen Grammatik empor und lutscht alle Nase lang wieder in sein geliebtes Platt zurück.
units.en:
There she was already, with her suitcases in front of her house –
'Hello!'
'You're here already?' said the princess – to the boundless amazement of the taxi driver, who took this for East Chinese. But it was Missingsch.
Missingsch is what comes out when a Low German speaker tries to speak High German. He clambers up the slippery polished staircase of German grammar and every few steps slides back down into his beloved Platt.
units.explain_en: 'Du bischa all do?' is dialect for 'Du bist ja schon da?' – don't learn this spelling! Missingsch mixes Plattdeutsch (Low German, the old language of northern Germany) with Hochdeutsch (standard German). 'Chauffeur' is old-fashioned; today it's 'Taxifahrer'. 'alle Nase lang' is a colloquial idiom for 'every few moments' – today 'ständig' or 'alle paar Minuten'. 'empor' is literary for 'nach oben' (upwards).

units.de: Lydia stammte aus Rostock, und sie beherrschte dieses Idiom in der Vollendung. Es ist kein bäurisches Platt – es ist viel feiner. Das Hochdeutsch darin nimmt sich aus wie Hohn und Karikatur; es ist, wie wenn ein Bauer in Frack und Zylinder aufs Feld ginge und so ackerte. Der Zylinder ischa en finen statschen Haut, över wen dor nich mit grot worn is, denn rutscht hei ümmer werrer aff, dat deiht he . . .
units.en: Lydia came from Rostock, and she had mastered this idiom to perfection. It isn't a peasant Platt – it's much finer. The High German in it comes across like mockery and caricature; it's as if a farmer went out to the field in tailcoat and top hat and ploughed like that. The top hat's a fine, stately hat, but if you haven't grown up with it, it keeps slipping off, that's what it does...
units.explain_en: 'stammen aus' = to come from (a place); today people also just say 'kommen aus'. 'beherrschen' = to master: 'Sie beherrscht drei Sprachen.' 'sich ausnehmen wie' is old-fashioned for 'wirken wie' (to seem like). 'wie wenn' = 'als ob' (as if) and takes Konjunktiv II: 'ginge'. The sentence 'Der Zylinder ischa en finen statschen Haut ...' is itself written in Missingsch as a demonstration. In standard German: 'Der Zylinder ist ja ein feiner, stattlicher Hut, aber wer damit nicht groß geworden ist, dem rutscht er immer wieder ab.'

Hier war eine Gelegenheit.
units.en: And then Platt holds all the humour of these northern Germans: their good-natured mockery when someone goes too far, their down-to-earth fun when they sniff out false glamour – and they do sniff it out, unfailingly... Lydia could speak this language when the occasion arose. Here was an occasion.
units.explain_en: 'es zu toll treiben' = to go too far (today: 'es übertreiben' or 'zu weit gehen'). 'wittern' means to sniff out, like an animal – literary; today 'merken' (to notice). 'der Spott' = mockery. 'die Gelegenheit' (opportunity, occasion) is a very useful word: 'bei Gelegenheit' = when there's a chance.

'verschlafen' (to oversleep) is a very useful word for school mornings. 'sich wundern' = to be surprised. 'der Dackel' (dachshund, a long dog) is her nickname for a long bag. 'lang gezogne' = 'lang gezogene'. 'pünktlich' = punctual.

Da wär immer Winter. Ische woll nich möchlich!« Frau Kremser war die Haushälterin der Prinzessin, Stubenmädchen, Reinmachefrau und Großsiegelbewahrerin. Gegen mich hatte sie noch immer, nach so langer Zeit, ein leise schnüffelndes Misstrauen – die Frau hatte einen guten Instinkt. »Sag mal . . . ist es wirklich so kalt da oben?«
units.en: 'Frau Kremser said,' Lydia began, 'I should take my fur and lots of warm coats – because there's no summer at all in Sweden, Frau Kremser said. It's always winter there. That can't be true!' Frau Kremser was the princess's housekeeper, chambermaid, cleaning lady and Keeper of the Great Seal. Even now, after such a long time, she still had a quiet, sniffing distrust of me – the woman had good instincts. 'Tell me... is it really that cold up there?'
units.explain_en: 'hat gesagt, ich soll ...' is everyday reported speech (formal written German would use 'ich solle'). 'Da wär immer Winter' – 'wär' = 'wäre', Konjunktiv for reported speech. 'Ische woll nich möchlich!' is Missingsch for 'Das ist wohl nicht möglich!' 'Großsiegelbewahrerin' (keeper of the great seal) is a joke royal title. 'Stubenmädchen' and 'Reinmachefrau' are old words; today: 'Putzfrau' or 'Reinigungskraft'. 'Sag mal ...' (Tell me ...) is used all the time.

units.en: It turned out that porter No. 47 came from Warnemünde, and there was no end of joy and chatter, until I broke up this idyll between people from the same region, because of the time. units.explain_en: 'Es ergab sich, dass ...' = 'It turned out that ...' (today: 'Es stellte sich heraus, dass ...'). A 'Gepäckträger' (porter) carried luggage at stations – a job that has mostly disappeared. 'der Zeit wegen' is old word order for 'wegen der Zeit'. 'sich unterhalten' = to chat – very useful. The Platt lines: 'Olln Döskopp! Heww di man nich so!' = 'Alter Dummkopf! Hab dich nicht so!' ('Hab dich nicht so!' – don't make such a fuss – is still common). 'Wi hemm noch bannig Tid!' = 'Wir haben noch viel Zeit!'

units.en: The princess claimed that I said to every woman I loved – and, for that matter, to every woman –: 'How lovely that you're here!' That was a whopping lie – sometimes I did also say or think: 'How lovely that you're there... and not here!' – but when I saw Lydia sitting next to me like that, then I really did say it. Why –?

'pfundsdick' is colloquial – 'Pfunds-' means 'huge' (compare 'ein Pfundskerl' = a great guy). 'die Lüge' = lie. 'neben mir' = next to me.

units.de: Das Plattdeutsche kann alles sein: zart und grob, humorvoll und herzlich, klar und nüchtern und vor allem, wenn man will, herrlich besoffen. Die Prinzessin bog sich diese Sprache ins Hochdeutsche um, wie es ihr passte – denn vom Missingschen gibt es hundert und aber hundert Abarten, von Friesland über Hamburg bis nach Pommern; da hat jeder kleine Ort seine Eigenheiten. Philologisch ist dem sehr schwer beizukommen; aber mit dem Herzen ist ihm beizukommen.
units.en: Low German can be anything: gentle and coarse, funny and warm-hearted, clear and sober and above all, if you like, gloriously drunk. The princess bent this language into High German however it suited her – because there are hundreds and hundreds of kinds of Missingsch, from Friesland via Hamburg to Pomerania; every little place has its own quirks. It's very hard to pin down scientifically; but you can get to it with your heart.
units.explain_en: 'nüchtern' means sober – both 'not drunk' and 'matter-of-fact'. 'besoffen' is slang for drunk – fine with friends. 'wie es ihr passte' = however it suited her; 'Das passt mir nicht' = 'That doesn't suit me'. 'hundert und aber hundert' is an old way of saying 'Hunderte und Aberhunderte'. 'einer Sache beikommen' (to get to grips with something) is old-fashioned.

units.en: So that was what the princess spoke – ah, not every day! That would have been unbearable. Sometimes, for a break, when she just felt like it, she spoke Missingsch; she used it to say the things that were especially close to her heart, and besides that, over time she had picked up a lot from Berlin. Und sprach:
»Einen weltbefohrnen dschungen Mann –!«
Und da war es aus. Und ich fand mich erst viel später bei ihr wieder, immer noch lachend, und mit der erotischen Weihe war es nichts geworden. Aber mit der Liebe war es etwas geworden.

And when I had explained everything to her, everything I knew at that moment – and that was quite a lot – and I was so proud of the daring things I'd said, and of how precisely and red-hot I had described and demonstrated it all, in words, so that now the moment had really come to say: 'Well, then...' – the princess gave me a long look. And said:
'Such a worldly young man –!'
And that was the end of that. And only much later did I come to my senses at her place, still laughing, and nothing had come of the erotic solemnity. But something had come of the love.
units.explain_en: Lydia's mock-posh line in Missingsch (standard German: 'Ein weltgewandter junger Mann!') makes him laugh so much that his big seduction speech collapses – and that's how they really fall in love. 'auseinandersetzen' here means 'to explain in detail' (today 'erklären'; 'sich auseinandersetzen mit' = to deal with). 'der Augenblick' = moment (today 'der Moment' is more common). 'Da war es aus' = then it was over. 'Aus etwas wird nichts' = something comes to nothing: 'Aus dem Ausflug wurde nichts.'

units.de:
Der Zug hielt.
Die Prinzessin fuhr auf, öffnete die Augen. »Wo sind wir?« – »Es sieht aus wie Stolp oder Stargard – jedenfalls ist es etwas mit St«, sagte ich. »Wie sieht es noch aus?« fragte sie. »Es sieht aus«, sagte ich und blickte auf die Backsteinhäuschen und den trübsinnigen Bahnhof, »wie wenn hier die Unteroffiziere geboren werden, die ihre Mannschaften schinden. Möchtest du hier Mittag essen?« Die Prinzessin schloss sofort die Augen. »Lydia«, sagte ich, »wir können auch im Speisewagen essen, der Zug hat einen.« – »Nein«, sagte sie. »Im Speisewagen werden die Kellner immer von der Geschwindigkeit des Zuges angesteckt, und es geht alles so furchtbar eilig – ich habe aber einen langsamen Magen . . . «
units.en: The train stopped. The princess started up and opened her eyes. 'Where are we?' – 'It looks like Stolp or Stargard – anyway, it's something beginning with St,' I said. 'What else does it look like?' she asked. 'It looks,' I said, glancing at the little brick houses and the gloomy station, 'like the sort of place where they breed the sergeants who bully their men. Would you like to have lunch here?' The princess shut her eyes at once. 'Lydia,' I said, 'we can also eat in the dining car; the train has one.' – 'No,' she said. 'In the dining car the waiters always catch the speed of the train, and everything is done in such a terrible hurry – but I've got a slow stomach...'
units.explain_en: The story continues on the train north. Stolp and Stargard were towns in Pomerania (today Słupsk and Stargard in Poland). ‘auffahren’ = to start up (from sleep). ‘trübsinnig’ = gloomy. ‘der Unteroffizier’ = non-commissioned officer, sergeant; ‘schinden’ = to treat cruelly – Tucholsky hated Prussian militarism. ‘der Speisewagen’ = dining car. ‘anstecken’ = to infect – here the waiters ‘catch’ the train's speed.

units.en: 'Fine. By the way, what are you reading, old girl?' – 'I've been sleeping on a fashionable novel for two hours. The only part of the body you can read it with...' and then she shut her eyes again. And opened them again. 'Look... that woman there! She's really misogynous!' – 'She's what?' – 'Misogynous... doesn't that mean scrawny? No, I've mixed it up with the pygmies; they're those people who live in trees... aren't they?' units.en: In Warnemünde, near where Lydia grew up, she explains every little house in her Low German dialect. They take the ferry to Denmark – Peter feels seasick while Lydia happily eats herring – and spend a few days in Copenhagen before crossing to Sweden. In Stockholm they hire an interpreter, Mr Bengtsson, an enormous, friendly man who speaks German with a strong American accent. For days he takes them around the countryside looking for a quiet, cheap little house, but they find nothing, and Lydia loses patience. At last Bengtsson has an idea: “We go to Mariefred.”

units.de:
Mariefred ist eine klitzekleine Stadt am Mälarsee. Es war eine stille und friedliche Natur, Baum und Wiese, Feld und Wald – niemand aber hätte von diesem Ort Notiz genommen, wenn hier nicht eines der ältesten Schlösser Schwedens wäre: das Schloss Gripsholm.
Es war ein strahlend heller Tag. Das Schloss, aus roten Ziegeln erbaut, stand leuchtend da, seine runden Kuppeln knallten in den blauen Himmel – dieses Bauwerk war dick, seigneural, eine bedächtige Festung. Bengtsson winkte dem Führer ab, Führer war er selber. Und wir gingen in das Schloss.
units.en: Mariefred is a teeny little town on Lake Mälaren. The countryside was quiet and peaceful – tree and meadow, field and forest – but nobody would ever have taken any notice of the place if it weren't for one of the oldest castles in Sweden: Gripsholm Castle. It was a brilliantly bright day. The castle, built of red bricks, stood there glowing, its round domes cracking into the blue sky – this building was stout, lordly, a slow and deliberate fortress. Bengtsson waved the guide away; he was the guide himself. And we went into the castle.
units.explain_en: Now we reach the place in the title. ‘klitzeklein’ = teeny-tiny (colloquial). ‘Notiz nehmen von’ = to take notice of. ‘der Ziegel’ = brick. ‘die Kuppel’ = dome. ‘knallen’ = to bang – the colours ‘bang’ against the sky. ‘seigneural’ (from French) = lordly. ‘bedächtig’ = slow and careful – a funny word for a building. ‘abwinken’ = to wave away.

units.de:
Viele schöne Gemälde hingen da. Mir sagten sie nichts. Ich kann nicht sehen. Es gibt Augenmenschen, und es gibt Ohrenmenschen, ich kann nur hören. Eine Achtelschwingung im Ton einer Unterhaltung: das weiß ich noch nach vier Jahren. Ein Gemälde? Das ist bunt. Ich weiß nichts vom Stil dieses Schlosses – ich weiß nur: wenn ich mir eins baute, so eins baute ich mir.
Herr Bengtsson erklärte uns das Schloss, wie er es seinen Amerikanern erklärt hätte, der Spiritus sang aus ihm, und nach jeder Jahreszahl sagte er: »Aber so genau weiß ich das nicht«, und dann sahen wir im Baedeker nach, und es war alles, alles falsch – und wir freuten uns mächtig.
units.en: Lots of beautiful paintings hung there. They meant nothing to me. I can't see. There are eye people and there are ear people; I can only hear. The tiniest shift in the tone of a conversation – I still remember that four years later. A painting? It's colourful. I know nothing about the style of this castle – I only know: if I built myself one, I'd build one like this. Mr Bengtsson explained the castle to us as he would have explained it to his Americans; the spirits sang out of him, and after every date he said: 'But I don't know that exactly,' and then we looked it up in the Baedeker, and it was all, all wrong – and we enjoyed ourselves enormously.
units.explain_en: ‘Mir sagten sie nichts’ = they meant nothing to me (‘Das sagt mir nichts’ is still common). ‘die Achtelschwingung’ = literally ‘an eighth of a vibration’, a tiny change. ‘die Jahreszahl’ = year, date. ‘der Spiritus sang aus ihm’ – he had been drinking (‘der Spiritus’ = spirit, alcohol). The Baedeker was the famous travel guidebook. ‘sich mächtig freuen’ = to be really pleased (‘mächtig’ = mightily, colloquial).

units.en: Bengtsson shows them a dungeon, a round cage for prisoners and a sweet little theatre inside the castle. Then Lydia insists: now or never. Bengtsson makes some phone calls and finds them rooms in a newer wing of the castle, rented out by a kind old lady who will also cook for them. The rooms are large and full of old castle furniture, with a view of the water and of a quiet park – and surprisingly cheap. They move in at once, delighted.

units.de:
Wir lagen auf der Wiese und baumelten mit der Seele.
Der Himmel war weiß gefleckt; wenn man von der Sonne recht schön angebraten war, kam eine Wolke, ein leichter Wind lief daher, und es wurde ein wenig kühl. Ein Hund trottete über das Gras, dahinten. »Was ist das für einer?« fragte ich. »Das ist ein Bulldackel«, sagte die Prinzessin. Und dann ließen wir wieder den Wind über uns hingehen und sagten gar nichts. Das ist schön, mit jemand schweigen zu können.
units.en: We lay on the meadow and let our souls dangle. The sky was dappled with white; whenever you'd been nicely roasted by the sun, a cloud came along, a light wind ran by, and it got a little cool. A dog trotted across the grass, over there. 'What kind is that?' I asked. 'That's a bull-dachshund,' said the princess. And then we let the wind blow over us again and said nothing at all. It's lovely to be able to be silent with someone.
units.explain_en: ‘Die Seele baumeln lassen’ (to let your soul dangle) is a popular German phrase for relaxing completely – and it comes from this book! ‘gefleckt’ = spotted, dappled. ‘anbraten’ = to fry lightly (a joke about sunbathing). ‘trotten’ = to trot. A ‘Bulldackel’ doesn't exist – Lydia invents it. ‘mit jemandem schweigen können’ = to be able to be silent with someone.

units.en: Lydia talks about her boss in Berlin, the “General Consul”, a soap manufacturer: fat, nosy, cowardly and gloating, a man who gets rich by simply not paying his bills. The real holidays begin, and they sleep deeply in the quiet castle. Chapter 2 opens somewhere else: in Läggesta, a children's home on the other side of the lake, run by a German woman. A nine-year-old girl stands alone at a window, enjoying a stolen moment of peace.

units.de:
Das Kind stand am Fenster und dachte so etwas wie: Wann hört dies auf? Dies hört nie auf. Wann hört dies auf?
Es hatte beide Arme auf das Fensterbrett gestützt, das durfte es nicht – aber es war für einen Augenblick, für einen winzigen, gestohlenen Augenblick, allein. Gleich würden die andern kommen; man spürte das zuerst im Rücken, der nun der Tür zugewendet war, der Rücken kitzelte erwartungsvoll. Wenn die andern kommen, ist es aus. Denn dann kommt sie.
units.en: The child stood at the window and thought something like: When will this stop? This will never stop. When will this stop? She had propped both arms on the windowsill, which she wasn't allowed to do – but for a moment, a tiny, stolen moment, she was alone. Soon the others would come; you felt that first in your back, which was now turned towards the door; your back tingled expectantly. When the others come, it's over. Because then she comes.
units.explain_en: Tucholsky calls the girl ‘das Kind’ and uses ‘es’ – in English we say ‘she’. ‘aufhören’ = to stop. ‘das Fensterbrett’ = windowsill. ‘stützen’ = to prop, lean. ‘Das durfte es nicht’ = she wasn't allowed to. ‘ein gestohlener Augenblick’ = a stolen moment. ‘kitzeln’ = to tickle. ‘Denn dann kommt sie’ – ‘sie’ is the director, whom the child fears.

units.de: Das kleine Mädchen schüttelte sich: es war wie die schnelle leise Bewegung eines Hundes, der Wasser abschüttelt. Das, was das Kind bedrückte, brauchte es nicht erst zu überdenken: es saß inmitten seiner kleinen Leiden wie auf einem Lotosblatt, zwischen andern Lotosblättern, und alle runden Blätter sahen es an – das Kind in der Mitte. Und es kannte sie alle, seine Leidensblätter.
units.en: The little girl gave herself a shake: it was like the quick, quiet movement of a dog shaking off water. She didn't need to think through what was weighing on her: she sat in the middle of her little sorrows as if on a lotus leaf, among other lotus leaves, and all the round leaves looked at her – the child in the middle. And she knew them all, her leaves of sorrow.
units.explain_en: ‘sich schütteln’ = to shake oneself. ‘abschütteln’ = to shake off. ‘bedrücken’ = to weigh on, depress (‘bedrückt’ = down, depressed). ‘überdenken’ = to think over. ‘inmitten’ (+ Genitiv) = in the middle of. ‘das Leiden’ = suffering, sorrow. ‘andern’ = ‘anderen’ – Tucholsky often drops the e.

units.en: The other children – her nickname ‘The Child’ – this children's home in Sweden – dead Will, and now the curve of fear rose, boiling red: Frau Adriani, red-haired Frau Adriani – and behind that the saddest thing of all: Mummy in Zurich. It was too much. The child was nine years old – it was too much for nine years. Now she cried the bitterest crying that children can cry: the kind that is cried inside and that nobody hears.

Trappeln. Schurren. Türenklappen. Kein Wort: eine stumme Schar näherte sich. Also war sie dabei. Du großer Gott –
Die Tür öffnete sich majestätisch, als habe sie sich allein aufgetan. Im Rahmen stand die Frau Direktor, der ›Teufelsbraten‹: die Adriani. Ihren Beinamen hatte sie von ihrem Lieblingsschimpfwort.
Sie war nicht sehr groß; eine stämmige, untersetzte Person, mit rötlichem Haar, graugrünlichen Augen und fast unsichtbaren Augenbrauen. Sie sprach schnell und hatte eine Art, die Leute anzusehn, die keinem guttat . . .
units.en: Tramping. Shuffling. Doors banging. Not a word: a silent crowd was approaching. So she was with them. Dear God – The door opened majestically, as if it had opened by itself. In the doorway stood the Director, the ‘Devil's Roast’: Frau Adriani. She got her nickname from her favourite term of abuse. She wasn't very tall; a sturdy, stocky person with reddish hair, greyish-green eyes and almost invisible eyebrows. She spoke quickly and had a way of looking at people that did nobody any good...
units.explain_en: ‘trappeln’, ‘schurren’ – sound words for small feet. ‘die Schar’ = crowd, flock. ‘die Frau Direktor’ is old usage; today ‘die Direktorin’. ‘der Teufelsbraten’ = little devil, rascal (literally ‘devil's roast’) – she calls the children that, so they call her that. ‘stämmig’ = sturdy. ‘anzusehn’ = ‘anzusehen’. ‘guttun’ = to do good.

units.en: Frau Adriani punishes the child for being upstairs: no supper. She runs the home for about forty girls, many of them German, through fear; she loves power more than anything. Back at the castle, Peter and Lydia read their letters, laze about and walk in the woods. One afternoon a group of German tourists arrives at the castle, and Peter has an idea for a prank. He climbs down a ladder into the old dungeon under a round wooden cover; Lydia pulls up the ladder, puts the cover back and hides. In the pitch dark, Peter hears the tourists come in above him.

»Hier ist nichts«, sagte eine Stimme. »Wahrscheinlich ein Brunnen – für die Belagerung oder so. Sehr interessant. Na, gehn wir weiter. Hier ist nichts.«
Hier wird gleich was sein.
»Huuuuuuu –« machte ich.
Oben wurde es totenstill. Die schleppenden Fußschritte waren verstummt. »Was war das?« sagte jemand. »Hast du das gehört?« – »Ja, mir war auch so – wahrscheinlich nur so ein Klang –«
»Huuuuuuu – aa – huuuuuuu –!« machte ich von neuem.
»Adolf, um Gottes willen – vielleicht ist hier ein Tier eingesperrt, ein Hund – komm weg!« – »Na, erlaube mal, das gibts doch nicht! Ist – ehö – ist da jemand?« – Ich blieb so still.
units.en: 'There's nothing here,' said a voice. 'Probably a well – for sieges or something. Very interesting. Well, let's move on. There's nothing here.' There's going to be something here in a moment. 'Whoooooo –' I went. Up above, it went deathly quiet. The dragging footsteps had stopped. 'What was that?' someone said. 'Did you hear that?' – 'Yes, I thought so too – probably just a sound –' 'Whoooooo – ah – whoooooo –!' I went again. 'Adolf, for heaven's sake – maybe there's an animal locked up here, a dog – come away!' – 'Oh, come on, that's impossible! Is – ahem – is anybody there?' – I kept completely still.
units.explain_en: ‘der Brunnen’ = well (also: fountain). ‘die Belagerung’ = siege. ‘gehn wir’ = ‘gehen wir’ (let's go). ‘totenstill’ = deathly quiet. ‘verstummen’ = to fall silent. ‘Mir war auch so’ = I thought so too. ‘um Gottes willen’ = for heaven's sake – very common. ‘eingesperrt’ = locked up. ‘Na, erlaube mal’ = oh, come on (surprised protest). ‘Das gibts doch nicht!’ = that's impossible! – very common today.

»Eine Täuschung«, sagte eine Männerstimme. »Komm – da war ja nichts«, sagte der andre der Männer. Und da dachte ich an die Löwen in den Zoologischen Gärten vor der Fütterung, holte tief Atem und begann zu röhren:
»Huuuuuu – brru – aa huuuuuuuuah!« –
Das war zu viel. »Hi!« kreischte oben eine Frau, und dann gab es ein eiliges Gestiefel, einer sagte noch schnell: »Aber das ist doch – das muss doch geklärt werden . . . werden gleich unten mal fragen . . . Unerhört – das ist doch . . . « – »Komm hier weg! Was müssen wir auch in alle Schlösser . . . « Fort waren sie. Da stand ich in meiner Dunkelheit. Mucksmäuschenstill.
units.en: 'Just an illusion,' said a man's voice. 'Come on – there was nothing there,' said the other man. And then I thought of the lions at the zoo before feeding time, took a deep breath and began to roar: 'Whoooooo – brrr – ah whoooooooah!' – That was too much. 'Eek!' shrieked a woman up above, and then there was a hurried clattering of boots, and someone quickly said: 'But this really – this must be looked into... we'll ask downstairs right away... Outrageous – this really is...' – 'Come away from here! Why do we have to go into every castle...' They were gone. There I stood in my darkness. As quiet as a mouse.
units.explain_en: ‘die Täuschung’ = illusion, deception. ‘tief Atem holen’ = to take a deep breath. ‘röhren’ = to roar (like a stag). ‘kreischen’ = to shriek. ‘das Gestiefel’ – a noun Tucholsky made up from ‘Stiefel’ (boots). ‘klären’ = to clear up, look into. ‘unerhört’ = outrageous. ‘mucksmäuschenstill’ = as quiet as a mouse – still used, especially with children.

units.en: For a moment Peter is afraid in the dark, until Lydia lifts the cover. He climbs out filthy and covered in cobwebs. Later, at coffee, the tourists – a Berlin company director called Teichmann and his party – invite the “German couple” to their table and ask nervously whether the castle is inhabited: they heard a wild animal in there. Peter says no, hardly any animals live there. Then Peter and Lydia walk out into the meadows, happy to be on holiday. Lydia, who has eyes like a lynx, spots a thin line of small figures coming along a narrow path.

units.de: Kinder waren es, kleine Mädchen, artig aufgereiht, wie Perlchen an der Schnur, immer zwei zu zwei. Eine herrisch aussehende Person ging an ihrer Spitze, sah sich öfter um – keines sprach. Nun waren sie nahe bei uns, wir traten beiseite und ließen den Zug vorüber. Die Führerperson warf uns einen glitzernden Blick zu. Die Kinder trappelten dahin. Wir sprachen nicht, als sie vorbeizogen.
units.en: They were children, little girls, neatly lined up like little pearls on a string, always two by two. A domineering-looking person walked at their head and often looked round – not one of them spoke. Now they were close to us; we stepped aside and let the line go by. The leader gave us a glittering look. The children tramped along. We didn't speak while they passed.
units.explain_en: ‘artig’ = well-behaved (old; today ‘brav’). ‘aufgereiht’ = lined up. ‘Perlchen an der Schnur’ = little beads on a string. ‘zwei zu zwei’ = in pairs (today ‘zu zweit’ or ‘paarweise’). ‘herrisch’ = domineering. ‘beiseitetreten’ = to step aside. ‘vorbeiziehen’ = to pass by (of a procession).

units.de: Ganz zum Schluss ging ein Kind allein; es ging, wie wenn es von jemandem gezogen würde, es hatte verweinte Augen, schluckte manchmal im Gehen vor sich hin, aber es weinte nicht. Sein Gesicht war auch nicht verschwollen, wie es verheulte Kinder haben . . . es sah vielmehr leer geweint aus, und in den bräunlichen Haaren lag ein goldner Schimmer.
units.en: Right at the end a child walked alone; she walked as if someone were pulling her; her eyes were red from crying, now and then she swallowed as she walked, but she wasn't crying. Her face wasn't swollen either, the way children's faces are after crying... rather, she looked cried out, empty, and there was a golden shimmer in her brownish hair.
units.explain_en: This is the child from the children's home – but Peter and Lydia don't know that yet. ‘verweint’ = red from crying. ‘schlucken’ = to swallow. ‘verschwollen’ = swollen. ‘verheult’ is colloquial for ‘verweint’ (heulen = to howl, cry). ‘leer geweint’ = cried out, emptied by crying. ‘goldner’ = ‘goldener’.

units.de: Es sah uns an, so müde und gleichgültig, wie es einen Baum angesehn hätte. In einem Anfall von Übermut und Kinderliebe steckte ihm die Prinzessin zwei kleine Glockenblumen, die wir gepflückt hatten, in die Hand. Das Kind zuckte zusammen, dann sah es auf, seine Lippen bewegten sich; es wollte vielleicht etwas sagen, danken . . . da drehte sich vorn die Person um, die Kleine beschleunigte ihre Schritte und hoppelte ängstlich der Schar nach. Staub und das Geräusch der marschierenden Kinderfüße. Dann war das Ganze vorüber.
units.en: She looked at us as tiredly and indifferently as she would have looked at a tree. In a fit of high spirits and love for children, the princess pressed two little bluebells we had picked into her hand. The child flinched, then looked up; her lips moved; perhaps she wanted to say something, to say thank you... then the person at the front turned round, the little one quickened her steps and hopped anxiously after the group. Dust and the sound of marching children's feet. Then it was all over.
units.explain_en: Remember the two bluebells – they will be important! ‘gleichgültig’ = indifferent. ‘der Anfall’ = fit, attack (‘ein Anfall von Übermut’ = a fit of high spirits). ‘die Glockenblume’ = bluebell (literally ‘bell flower’). ‘pflücken’ = to pick (flowers). ‘zusammenzucken’ = to flinch. ‘beschleunigen’ = to speed up. ‘hoppeln’ = to hop (like a rabbit).

units.en: Lydia wishes she could see the northern lights, so the two of them stare at the pale sky and imagine one together – for a moment they truly see it. Back at the castle, the landlady, Frau Andersson, explains in her own funny German that the girls belong to the children's home at Läggesta. Its German director is “not a good lady”: she hits the children – not hard enough for the police to act, but they are terrified of her. That night at Läggesta the child lies awake. Her father left long ago; her mother in Switzerland sent her here because it is cheaper. When a maid secretly posted her begging letters, the maid was sacked. Her little brother Will died of flu and lies buried in the churchyard at Mariefred.

units.de:
Der Bruder nicht. Mutti nicht. Vater weggegangen, wohin . . . Niemand war da. Das Kind war allein. Es dachte das Wort nicht – viel schlimmer: es fühlte die Einsamkeit, wie nur Kinder sie fühlen können.
Die kleinen Mädchen raschelten in den Kissen. Eins flüsterte im Schlaf. Das war jetzt der zweite Sommer hier oben. Es würde nie anders werden. Nie. Mutti soll kommen, dachte das Kind. Aber sie müsste es hier fortnehmen, denn gegen Frau Adriani kam auch Mutti nicht auf. Niemand kam gegen sie auf.
units.en: Not her brother. Not Mummy. Father gone away, who knows where... No one was there. The child was alone. She didn't think the word – much worse: she felt the loneliness, as only children can feel it. The little girls rustled in their pillows. One whispered in her sleep. This was her second summer up here now. It would never be any different. Never. Mummy must come, thought the child. But she would have to take her away from here, because not even Mummy could stand up to Frau Adriani. No one could stand up to her.
units.explain_en: ‘die Einsamkeit’ = loneliness. ‘rascheln’ = to rustle. ‘flüstern’ = to whisper. ‘Es würde nie anders werden’ = it would never change. ‘fortnehmen’ = to take away (today ‘wegnehmen’, ‘wegholen’). ‘gegen jemanden aufkommen’ = to hold one's own against someone. ‘Mutti’ = Mummy – still common.

units.de: Schritte? Wenn sie jetzt käme? Einmal war Gertie krank gewesen; da war Frau Adriani fünf Mal in der Nacht heraufgekommen – fünf Mal hatte sie nach dem kranken Kind gesehen, sie hatte fast eifersüchtig mit der Krankheit gekämpft. Und zum Schluss hatte sie das Fieber besiegt. Wenn sie jetzt käme? Nichts – eins der acht Betten hatte geknarrt. Das war Lisa Wedigen, die schlief immer so unruhig.
units.en: Footsteps? What if she came now? Once, when Gertie had been ill, Frau Adriani had come up five times in the night – five times she had looked in on the sick child; she had fought the illness almost jealously. And in the end she had beaten the fever. What if she came now? Nothing – one of the eight beds had creaked. That was Lisa Wedigen, who always slept so restlessly.
units.explain_en: Tucholsky shows that even Frau Adriani cares in her own way – she wants to win against everything, even illness. ‘Wenn sie jetzt käme?’ = What if she came now? (Konjunktiv II). ‘nach jemandem sehen’ = to look in on someone. ‘eifersüchtig’ = jealous. ‘besiegen’ = to defeat. ‘knarren’ = to creak. ‘unruhig’ = restless.

units.en: Chapter 3. A letter arrives from Karlchen, Peter's best friend since they served together in the First World War. Karlchen works at a tax office in the Rhineland: a quiet, utterly reliable man who loves nonsense. Peter and Lydia bend over the letter and read it together:

units.de:
Lieber Freund!
Ich habe in diesem Jahr noch acht Tage Urlaub gut und würde die gern mit Dir und Deiner lieben Frau Freundin verleben. Wie ich höre, seid Ihr in Schweden. Lieber Freund, würdest Du wohl Deinen alten Kriegskameraden, der Dir in so manchem Granattrichter den Steigbügel gehalten hat, bei Euch aufnehmen? Lieber Freund, ich zahle auch das Reisegeld für mich allein; es ist mir sehr schmerzlich, für mich allein etwas bezahlen zu müssen; es ist dies sonst nicht meine Art, wie Du weißt. Schreibe mir bitte, wie ich zu Euch fahre, lieber Freund.
units.en: Dear friend! I still have eight days' holiday owing to me this year and would love to spend them with you and your dear lady friend. I hear you are in Sweden. Dear friend, would you take in your old war comrade, who held your stirrup for you in many a shell crater? Dear friend, I will even pay my own fare; it is very painful for me to have to pay for something for myself; as you know, that is not usually my way. Please write and tell me how to get to you, dear friend.
units.explain_en: Karlchen's letter is full of jokes. ‘Urlaub gut haben’ = to have holiday owing. ‘verleben’ = to spend (time) – today ‘verbringen’. ‘die Frau Freundin’ is a mock-polite way of saying girlfriend. ‘jemandem den Steigbügel halten’ = to hold someone's stirrup, i.e. help them – but nobody rides a horse in a shell crater! ‘der Granattrichter’ = shell crater. He pretends it hurts him to pay for himself.

units.en: Karlchen arrives and gets on with Lydia straight away, and Peter enjoys their friendship: “friendship is like home”. The newspapers bring back the worries of the times, and Lydia tells them that her boss once kept her late at the office to ask her to be his girlfriend; she said no. Meanwhile at Läggesta, Frau Adriani catches a girl, Lisa Wedigen, hiding food and punishes the whole home. A few days later the three friends walk past the children's home. A door bangs, and a little girl comes running out – straight into their arms. It is the child with the bluebells. She sobs that her name is Ada Collin, that Frau Adriani hits them and that she wants to go to her Mummy in Zurich. But before she can give the address, she cries: “She's coming!”

units.en: Frau Adriani drags Ada into the house and locks the door. Lydia tells the two men they are donkeys: they can't start a war, but they must help the child – and she has whispered to Ada to smuggle out her mother's address on a slip of paper in half an hour. While they wait on the grass, they hear a woman shrieking inside the house. Peter slips into a dark daydream about the cruel crowds in a Roman arena and is shocked to feel the same wish to make this woman suffer, which he pushes away. Then they creep back towards the house, Karlchen from one side, Peter and Lydia from the other.

units.en: 'Shh!' went the princess. Nothing. Karlchen was nowhere to be seen. I looked at her questioningly. We walked on slowly, treading carefully, as if we were walking on ice. Was that a face behind a window – a perfectly round disc...? An illusion; it was a reflection. We walked close past the house. The princess was looking around everywhere. Suddenly she went forward – 'Quick!' she said – and ran towards a white spot in the grass not far from the house... there lay a small piece of paper. At the back, Karlchen was strolling slowly along the fence. The princess bent down, looked at the paper, picked it up and walked quickly on.

units.en: Back at the castle the three of them write fourteen drafts before sending Lydia's clear, sensible letter to Frau Collin in Zurich. Karlchen's holiday ends; he leaves, and the next day four crazy postcards arrive from him. Then Lydia's old friend Billie (Sibylle) comes to stay – a sporty, lively young woman whom Peter secretly admires. Frau Collin writes back, grateful: they should go and talk to Frau Adriani. Peter and Lydia buy Ada a doll in Swedish costume and go to the home, while Billie waits in the woods. Frau Adriani receives them coldly and suspiciously, but she sends for the child.

units.en: Before Ada is taken away, Peter quickly tells her: “If you ever need to tell your Mummy something important, we live at Gripsholm Castle!” Frau Adriani throws them out, threatening to call the police. The friends visit little Will's tiny grave, and Peter cries. That evening they phone Zurich: Frau Collin agrees to send a letter allowing them to take Ada away, together with a cheque. Billie stays a few more days, and the three of them grow very close; then Billie leaves, and Peter and Lydia's last days begin. Frau Collin's letter still hasn't come. At last it arrives. Then, during lunch, the landlady hurries in:

Da stand der kleine Gegenstand.
Sie sah recht zerrupft aus, verweint, die Haare hingen ihr ins Gesicht, vielleicht war sie schnell gelaufen. Das Kind war nicht recht bei sich. units.en: There stood the little object. She looked quite dishevelled and tear-stained, her hair hanging in her face; perhaps she had been running fast. The child wasn't quite herself. When she saw Lydia, she ran straight to her and hid her face in her dress. 'What's the matter? What is it?' The princess bent down and changed from the sporty girl of that morning into a mummy – no, she was both. The castle landlady stood by, a sponge of curiosity – she soaked it all up. Well?

units.en: Peter and Lydia decide they will never hand Ada back. Frau Adriani telephones and threatens to report them for kidnapping unless the child is returned within half an hour. Peter calmly promises to come. They have to take Ada with them to collect her things, and she is terrified. At the home, Frau Adriani speaks to Ada in a falsely sweet voice, refuses to let her off her punishment, and tells Peter and Lydia to bring up their own children instead. She thinks she has won.

units.en: I looked her firmly in the eyes... for a moment longer I let her wriggle in her insane, impatient rage. Her quick eyes kept darting from us to the child and back; she was waiting for the child. I thought about how many people in the world might be in the power of women like her, and what it would be like if we really had to leave the child to her, and what the other children here had to put up with... 'So – now I shall make the necessary arrangements...' Frau Adriani stood up. Then I struck.

units.en: When she sees the cheque, Frau Adriani suddenly becomes cold and businesslike and demands extra money for things the child has supposedly broken. Peter refuses. Then she tries tears – she is a hard-working woman, a mother to the children – and when that doesn't work either, she swears at them. They go upstairs to pack Ada's things while frightened girls peer out of every door. When Frau Adriani steps towards Ada, Peter moves between them. Looking into her eyes, he understands what drives her: a hunger for power.

units.de: Das Mädchen kam mit dem Koffer; wir packten, schweigend. Einmal riss die Frau ein Hemdchen an sich und warf es wieder hin. Das Kind hielt die Hand der Prinzessin. Die Mädchen in ihrer Ecke atmeten kaum. Frau Adriani sah zu ihnen hinüber und ruckte mit dem Kopf, da gingen sie schlurfend zur Tür hinaus. Der Koffer wurde geschlossen. Wir trugen ihn hinunter. Ein Mädchen wollte uns helfen – Frau Adriani verbot es mit einer Handbewegung. Der Koffer war nicht schwer. Das Kind ging eilig mit; es weinte nicht mehr. Ich hörte es einmal tief aufatmen.
units.en: The maid came with the suitcase; we packed in silence. Once the woman snatched up a little shirt and threw it down again. The child held the princess's hand. The girls in their corner hardly breathed. Frau Adriani looked over at them and jerked her head, and they shuffled out of the door. The suitcase was closed. We carried it downstairs. A girl wanted to help us – Frau Adriani forbade it with a wave of her hand. The suitcase wasn't heavy. The child walked quickly along with us; she wasn't crying any more. Once I heard her take a deep breath of relief.

»Die Quittung?« Frau Adriani ging auf ihren Tisch zu, schrieb etwas auf ein Blatt und reichte es mir, wie mit der Feuerzange. Um ein Haar hätte sie mir leidgetan, aber ich wusste, wie gefährlich dieses Mitleid war und wie verschwendet. Es hätte ihr nicht einmal gutgetan, denn von diesem Seelenhonorar kauft sie sich neue Kulissen, und alles fängt wieder von vorn an. Ich gab ihr den Scheck. Ich sah auf ihr Gesicht. Der Vorhang war heruntergelassen – jetzt wurde nicht mehr gespielt. Das Stück war aus.
Langsam gingen wir aus dem Hause, in dem das Kind so viel gelitten hatte.
Keiner von uns sah mehr zurück. Die Haustür wurde geschlossen.
units.en: 'The receipt?' Frau Adriani went to her desk, wrote something on a sheet of paper and handed it to me as if with fire tongs. She very nearly made me feel sorry for her, but I knew how dangerous that pity was, and how wasted. It wouldn't even have done her any good, because with this payment for her soul she buys herself new scenery, and everything starts all over again. I gave her the cheque. I looked at her face. The curtain had come down – there was no more acting now. The play was over. Slowly we walked out of the house in which the child had suffered so much. None of us looked back. The front door was closed.

units.en: The last day of the holiday. Peter wonders why they don't just stay at Gripsholm forever, but he knows that worries would follow them: a place is only beautiful for those passing through. They say goodbye to the landlady and take the little train to Stockholm with Ada, who slowly tells them everything she went through. On the long journey home Lydia mothers her. Peter thinks their five weeks together were perfect, without a single quarrel – “anyone can manage a short happiness”. At night in Trelleborg the train is pushed onto the ferry, and a brightly lit passenger ship glides past with music playing.

Dann stand unser Wagen auf der Fähre. Das Schiff erzitterte leise. Die Lichter an der Küste wurden immer kleiner und kleiner, dann versanken sie in der blauen Nachtluft.
Wir standen an Deck. Die Prinzessin sog den salzigen Atem des Meeres ein. »Daddy – ich bedanke mich auch schön für diesen Sommer!« – »Nein, Alte – ich bedanke mich bei dir!« Sie sah über die dunkle See. »Das Meer . . . « sagte sie leise, »das Meer . . . « Hinter uns lag Schweden, Schweden und ein Sommer.
units.en: Then our carriage stood on the ferry. The ship trembled softly. The lights on the coast grew smaller and smaller, then they sank into the blue night air. We stood on deck. The princess breathed in the salty breath of the sea. 'Daddy – thank you so much for this summer!' – 'No, old girl – I'm the one who thanks you!' She looked out over the dark sea. 'The sea...' she said quietly, 'the sea...' Behind us lay Sweden, Sweden and a summer.
units.explain_en: A quiet goodbye. ‘der Wagen’ here = railway carriage. ‘erzittern’ = to tremble. ‘versinken’ = to sink. ‘an Deck’ = on deck. ‘einsaugen’ = to breathe in, suck in. ‘sich bedanken für’ = to say thank you for – very useful. ‘Daddy’ is Lydia's pet name for Peter. ‘die See’ = the sea (feminine!), but ‘der See’ = the lake.

Später saßen wir im Speisesaal in einer Ecke und aßen und tranken. »Auf den Urlaub, Alte!« – »Auf was noch?«
»Auf Karlchen!« – »Hoch!«
»Auf Billie!« – »Hoch!«
»Auf die Adriani!« – »Nieder!«
»Auf deinen Generalkonsul!« – »Mittelhoch!«
»Das sind alles keine Trinksprüche, Daddy. Weißt du keinen andern? Du weißt einen andern. Na?«
Ich wusste, was sie meinte. »Martje Flor«, sagte ich.
»Martje Flor!«
units.en: Later we sat in a corner of the dining room, eating and drinking. 'To the holiday, old girl!' – 'And to what else?' 'To Karlchen!' – 'Cheers!' 'To Billie!' – 'Cheers!' 'To Adriani!' – 'Down with her!' 'To your General Consul!' – 'Half cheers!' 'Those aren't proper toasts, Daddy. Don't you know another one? You do know another one. Well?' I knew what she meant. 'Martje Flor,' I said. 'Martje Flor!'
units.explain_en: They drink toasts to everyone in the story. ‘Auf …!’ = (Here's) to …! ‘Hoch!’ = cheers, hurrah (from ‘Er lebe hoch!’); ‘Nieder!’ = down with …; ‘Mittelhoch’ (half-cheers) is Peter's joke. ‘der Trinkspruch’ = toast. Martje Flor is the heroine of a North Frisian legend – the next part explains who she was.

units.de:
Das war jene friesische Bauerntochter gewesen, die im Dreißigjährigen Kriege von den Landsknechten an den Tisch gezerrt wurde; sie hatten alles ausgeräubert, den Weinkeller und die Räucherkammer, die Obstbretter und den Wäscheschrank, und der Bauer stand daneben und rang die Hände. Roh hatten sie das Mädchen herbeigeholt – he! da stand sie, trotzig und gar nicht verängstigt. Sie sollte einen Trinkspruch ausbringen! Und warfen dem Bauern eine Flasche an den Kopf und drückten ihr ein volles Glas in die Hand.
Da hob Martje Flor Stimme und Glas, und es wurde ganz still in dem kleinen Zimmer, als sie ihre Worte sagte, und alle Niederdeutschen kennen sie.
»Up dat es uns wohl goh up unsre ohlen Tage –!« sagte sie.
units.en: She was that Frisian farmer's daughter who, in the Thirty Years' War, was dragged to the table by mercenaries; they had plundered everything, the wine cellar and the smokehouse, the fruit shelves and the linen cupboard, and the farmer stood by wringing his hands. They had roughly fetched the girl – hey! there she stood, defiant and not frightened at all. She was to propose a toast! And they threw a bottle at the farmer's head and pressed a full glass into her hand. Then Martje Flor raised her voice and her glass, and the little room went completely quiet as she spoke her words, and all North Germans know them. 'May all be well with us in our old days –!' she said.
units.explain_en: The last words of the book are in Low German – in standard German: ‘Auf dass es uns wohlgehe in unseren alten Tagen!’ (May we be well in our old age). It's a wish for a love that lasts. ‘der Landsknecht’ = mercenary soldier. ‘ausräubern’ = to plunder. ‘die Hände ringen’ = to wring one's hands. ‘trotzig’ = defiant. ‘einen Trinkspruch ausbringen’ = to propose a toast.
